latin.503: GAR. Resp. 1. Eadem subtilitate ostendi posse, per illud peccatum, non esse intelligendum (quod tamen volunt qui his rationibus utuntur) corruptionem haereditariam, unicuique nostrum ab origine inhaerentem. Nam ea corruptio non potest dici intrare in nos: cum sit innata & ingenita, & penetissime infita a principio in natura nostra: illud autem intrare aliquo dicitur, quod foris eo delatum est, aut venit aliunde, & antea ibi non erat. Certe nemo nostrum prius fuit, quam fuit corruptus.
latin.504: PLAC. Eadem quidem esset subtilitas, si posset argumentum meum aeque corruptioni ac peccato actuali accommodari: nunc vero cum haec viri docti subtilitas in argumento a meo valde diverso sita sit, intelligere non possum, cur eadem subtilitas dicatur, aut quid argumentis meis noceat? Quanquam vim nullam habet. Quis enim non videt per illum peccati introitum non esse intelligendum introitum situm in motu locali qui proprius est corporum & substantiarum?
latin.505: Quis etiam, nisi sit Pelagianus, non intelligit peccatum intrasse in homines propagatione naturali simul ac gignimur, ac proinde in genitos non fuisse foris delatum? nempe dicitur in nos intrasse, quia revera intra nos est, nec tamen est a creatione, aut ab ipsa humana natura, sed aliunde, a tentatione serpentis & peccato primi hominis actuali. Itaque revera per unum hominem vitium illud in naturam humanam ubi antea non erat, nec esse debebat, intravit, & una cum natura in nos omnes, id quod de peccato actuali dici non potest. Quod igitur innatum est, id si non est a natura, quominus per parentes in liberos introiisse dicatur, nihil potest prohibere. Sic potest dici per parentem in liberos lepra aut podagra intraisse, quamvis lepra insit liberis ab ortu. Non quidem prius tempore, at prius tamen natura fuimus quam corrupti fuimus. Non potest enim corruptio naturae non esse posterior ipsa natura. Caeterum si prius non fuimus quam corrupti fuimus, & corruptio sequitur, Non entis nulla sunt accidentia.
latin.506: GAR. 2. Non est absurdius si dicatur peccatum, aut actio singularis Adae introiisse, quam si dicatur Christi justitia introisse. At ita loquitur Clar. Amyr. in paraphrasi huius versus, per unum hominem qui Iesus Christus est, vera justitia introducta est in mundum, quod de justitia imputata, non minus quam de inhaerente dicitur. Quibus non displicet si dicatur justitia imputata introduci vel intrare, quidni placeat, si dicatur etiam, peccatum imputatum introire?
latin.507: PLAC. Dixitne Clar. Amyr. justitiam quae Christo inhaesit, per eum unum in homines intrasse? Non certe: Attamen id ab eo dici oportuit, ut posset eius locutione expositio viri docti defendi. Nempe justitiae nomine, quae per unum hominem in mundum introducta est, aut vehementer fallor, aut cum Calvino remissionem peccatorum intellexit, eamque introductam voluit non in omnes homines, aut in omnes credentes sola imputatione, sed impetratam a Christo & donatam a Patre & praedicatione Evangelii oblatam omnibus & fide acceptam a credentibus, in quibus constans permanet: id quod de actuali Adae peccato dici similiter non potest.
latin.508: GAR. 3. Quod sine introduci dicitur saepius, quod tum demum esse incipit, ut apud Graecos εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον εἰσελθεῖν intrare in iudicium, est incipere litem. Et Christus dicitur intrasse, & introductus fuisse in mundum, cum in mundo incepit esse secundum humanitatem suam. Act. 1. 21. Heb. 1. 6. Ergo cum peccatum incepit esse primum in genere humano, quod fuit per primorum parentum inobedientiam, merito dicitur in mundum intrasse.

pass_a.503: GAR Resp. 1: By the same subtlety one can show that 'that sin' need not mean (as those who use these reasons want) the hereditary corruption inhering in each of us from birth. For that corruption cannot be said to enter us: it is innate and inborn, deeply fixed from the start in our nature; but a thing is said to enter a place when it is brought there from outside, or comes from elsewhere, and was not there before. Certainly none of us existed before he was corrupt.
pass_a.504: PLAC: That would be the same subtlety if my argument fitted corruption as well as actual sin. As it is, the learned man's subtlety sits in an argument far from mine—I cannot see why call it the same, or how it hurts mine. It has no force anyway. Who does not see that sin's 'entry' is not local motion proper to bodies and substances?
pass_a.505: Who but a Pelagian fails to see sin entered humans by natural propagation as we are begotten—and so was not fetched from outside into those already born? It is said to have entered us because it truly is inside us, yet not from creation or human nature itself, but from elsewhere: the serpent's temptation and the first man's actual. So through one man that vice entered human nature where it was not and ought not to be, and with nature into us all—which cannot be said of the actual. What is innate, if not from nature, may still be said to have entered children through parents: as leprosy or gout through a parent, though the child has leprosy from birth. Not earlier in time, yet earlier by nature we were than we were corrupt—corruption of nature cannot but be later than nature. If we were not before we were corrupt, and corruption follows: of a non-being there are no accidents.
pass_a.506: GAR 2: It is no more absurd to say Adam's sin or singular act entered than to say Christ's righteousness entered. So Amyraut paraphrases this verse: through one man, Jesus Christ, true righteousness was introduced into the world—said of imputed righteousness no less than of inhering. If imputed righteousness may be said to be introduced or enter, why not imputed sin also?
pass_a.507: PLAC: Did Amyraut say the righteousness that inhered in Christ entered humans through him alone? Certainly not—yet that is what would be needed to shore up the learned man's reading by his phrase. By 'righteousness introduced through one man into the world' he meant, unless I am badly wrong, with Calvin the remission of sins: not brought into all humans, or into all believers by imputation alone, but obtained by Christ, given by the Father, offered to all in the Gospel's preaching, received by faith in believers, and abiding there—which cannot likewise be said of Adam's actual.
pass_a.508: GAR 3: What is said to be introduced often means what then first begins to be—as among the Greeks εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον εἰσελθεῖν, to enter into judgment, is to begin a suit. And Christ is said to have entered and been introduced into the world when he began to be in the world according to his humanity (Acts 1:21; Heb 1:6). Therefore when sin first began to be in the human race—through the first parents' disobedience—it is rightly said to have entered the world. Tip before PLAC's reply.

503: GAR. Resp. 1. By the same subtlety it can be shown that by that sin is not to be understood (which yet those who use these reasons want) the hereditary corruption inhering in each of us from origin. For that corruption cannot be said to enter into us: since it is innate and inborn, and most deeply fixed from the beginning in our nature: but that is said to enter somewhere, which has been brought there from outside, or comes from elsewhere, and before was not there. Certainly none of us was earlier than he was corrupt.
504: PLAC. It would indeed be the same subtlety, if my argument could be accommodated equally to corruption and to actual sin: but now since this subtlety of the learned man is situated in an argument very diverse from mine, I cannot understand why it is called the same subtlety, or what it harms in my arguments? Although it has no force. For who does not see that by that entry of sin is not to be understood an entry situated in local motion which is proper to bodies and substances?
505: Who also, unless he is a Pelagian, does not understand that sin entered into humans by natural propagation as soon as we are begotten, and therefore was not brought from outside into those already born? namely it is said to have entered into us, because it truly is inside us, and yet is not from creation, or from human nature itself, but from elsewhere, from the serpent's temptation and the first man's actual sin. And so truly through one man that vice entered into human nature where before it was not, nor ought to be, and together with nature into us all, which cannot be said of actual sin. What therefore is innate, if it is not from nature, nothing can prohibit that it be said to have entered through parents into children. So it can be said that through a parent leprosy or gout entered into children, although leprosy is in the children from birth. Not indeed earlier in time, but earlier yet by nature we were than we were corrupt. For corruption of nature cannot but be later than nature itself. But if we were not earlier than we were corrupt, and corruption follows, Of a non-being there are no accidents.
506: GAR. 2. It is not more absurd if it is said that sin, or Adam's singular action, entered, than if it is said that Christ's righteousness entered. But so speaks the distinguished Amyraut in a paraphrase of this verse: through one man who is Jesus Christ, true righteousness was introduced into the world, which is said of imputed righteousness no less than of inhering. To those whom it does not displease if imputed righteousness is said to be introduced or to enter, why should it not please, if imputed sin also is said to enter?
507: PLAC. Did the distinguished Amyraut say that the righteousness which inhered in Christ entered through him alone into humans? Certainly not: And yet that ought to have been said by him, so that by his locution the learned man's exposition could be defended. Namely by the name of righteousness which through one man was introduced into the world, either I am badly mistaken, or with Calvin he understood the remission of sins, and wished it introduced not into all humans, or into all believers by imputation alone, but obtained by Christ and given by the Father and offered to all by the preaching of the Gospel and accepted by faith by believers, in whom it remains constant: which cannot similarly be said of Adam's actual sin.
508: GAR. 3. What is often said to be introduced is that which then at last begins to be, as among the Greeks eis to dikasterion eiselthein, to enter into judgment, is to begin a suit. And Christ is said to have entered, and to have been introduced into the world, when in the world he began to be according to his humanity. Acts 1. 21. Heb. 1. 6. Therefore when sin first began to be in the human race, which was through the first parents' disobedience, it is rightly said to have entered into the world.
